paragraphs: Religion, when considered in relation to society (which is either general or particular), can also be divided into two kinds: the religion of man and the religion of the citizen. The first has no temples, altars or rites. It is limited to the purely inward worship of the supreme God and the eternal duties of morality. It is the religion of the Gospel, pure and simple, true theism, what we may call natural divine right or law. The other kind is established in a single country and gives that country its gods, its own guardian patrons. It has its dogmas, its rites, and an outward worship prescribed by law. Outside the one nation that follows it, the whole world is in its eyes unbelieving, foreign and barbarous; it extends the duties and rights of man only as far as its own altars. All the religions of early peoples were of this kind, and we may define it as civil or positive divine right or law.

There is a third kind of religion, a stranger one, which gives people two codes of law, two rulers and two countries. It subjects them to contradictory duties and makes it impossible for them to be faithful both to religion and to citizenship. Such are the religion of the Lamas and that of the Japanese, and such is Roman Christianity, which may be called the religion of the priest. It produces a sort of mixed and anti-social code that has no name.

Viewed politically, all three kinds of religion have their defects. The third is so plainly bad that it is a waste of time to stop and prove it. Everything that destroys social unity is worthless; every institution that sets a man in contradiction with himself is worthless.

The second kind is good because it joins the worship of the gods to love of the laws. It makes the country the object of the citizens’ devotion and teaches them that serving the State is serving its guardian god. It is a form of theocracy, in which there can be no pontiff but the prince and no priests but the magistrates. To die for one’s country then becomes martyrdom; to break its laws is impiety; and to expose a guilty man to public curses is to hand him over to the anger of the gods: _Sacer estod_.

On the other hand, it is bad because it is founded on lies and error. It deceives men, makes them credulous and superstitious, and drowns the true worship of the Divinity in empty ceremony. It is bad again when it becomes tyrannical and exclusive and makes a people bloodthirsty and intolerant, so that it breathes fire and slaughter and regards the killing of anyone who does not believe in its gods as a sacred act. The result is to put such a people in a natural state of war with all others, which seriously endangers its own security.

What remains, then, is the religion of man, or Christianity. I do not mean the Christianity of today but that of the Gospel, which is entirely different. Through this holy, sublime and true religion, all men are children of one God and recognize one another as brothers, and the society that unites them is not dissolved even by death.

But this religion has no particular relation to the body politic. It leaves the laws with the force they have in themselves and adds nothing to it, and so one of the great bonds that hold a particular society together fails to work. Worse still, far from binding the hearts of the citizens to the State, it draws them away from all earthly things. I know of nothing more contrary to the social spirit.

We are told that a people of true Christians would form the most perfect society imaginable. I see only one great difficulty in this supposition: a society of true Christians would not be a society of men.

I say further that such a society, for all its perfection, would be neither the strongest nor the most lasting. Its very perfection would rob it of its bond of union; the flaw that would destroy it would lie in that perfection itself.

Everyone would do his duty. The people would obey the laws, the rulers would be just and moderate, the magistrates upright and incorruptible; the soldiers would scorn death; there would be neither vanity nor luxury. So far, so good; but let us hear more.

Christianity as a religion is entirely spiritual and concerned only with heavenly things; the Christian’s country is not of this world. He does his duty, it is true, but he does it with deep indifference to whether his efforts succeed or fail. Provided he has nothing to reproach himself with, it matters little to him whether things go well or badly here on earth. If the State is prosperous, he hardly dares to share in the public happiness, for fear of growing proud of his country’s glory; if the State is declining, he blesses the hand of God that lies heavy on His people.

For the State to be peaceful and for harmony to be maintained, all the citizens without exception would have to be good Christians. If by bad luck there were a single self-seeker or hypocrite, a Catiline or a Cromwell, for instance, he would certainly get the better of his pious fellow citizens. Christian charity does not readily allow a man to think badly of his neighbors. As soon as he has found, by some trick, the art of deceiving them and seizing a share of public authority, you have a man established in dignity; it is the will of God that he be respected. Very soon you have a power; it is God’s will that it be obeyed. And if the one who holds that power abuses it, it is the scourge with which God punishes His children. There would be scruples about driving out the usurper: public peace would have to be disturbed, violence used and blood shed; all this fits badly with Christian meekness. And after all, in this valley of sorrows, what does it matter whether we are free men or slaves? The essential thing is to get to heaven, and resignation is only one more means of doing so.

If war breaks out with another State, the citizens go readily out to battle; not one of them thinks of flight. They do their duty, but they have no passion for victory; they know better how to die than how to conquer. What does it matter to them whether they win or lose? Does not Providence know better than they what is good for them? Only think what use a proud, impetuous and passionate enemy could make of their stoicism! Set against them those generous peoples who were consumed by burning love of glory and of their country; imagine your Christian republic face to face with Sparta or Rome. The pious Christians will be beaten, crushed and destroyed before they know where they are, or will owe their safety only to the contempt their enemy conceives for them. In my view it was a fine oath that the soldiers of Fabius took, who swore not to conquer or die but to come back victorious — and kept their oath. Christians would never have taken such an oath; they would have seen it as tempting God.

But I am mistaken in speaking of a Christian republic; the two terms exclude each other. Christianity preaches only servitude and dependence. Its spirit is so favorable to tyranny that tyranny always profits from such a _régime_. True Christians are made to be slaves; they know it and do not much mind, because this short life counts for too little in their eyes.
